Part I · Lecture 1

Problem solving by searching

Problem-solving agents Russell & Norvig

Imagine an agent in Arad, Romania, on a touring holiday. Its performance measure has many parts: improve its suntan, improve its Romanian, take in the sights, enjoy the nightlife, avoid hangovers. But it holds a non-refundable ticket out of Bucharest tomorrow, so it sensibly adopts one goal: get to Bucharest.

Goal formulation, based on the current situation and the performance measure, is the first step in problem solving. A goal is a set of world states; it lets the agent ignore actions that cannot achieve it.

Problem formulation is the next step: deciding which actions and states to consider, given the goal. Here the useful level of detail is “drive from one major town to the next”, not “turn the steering wheel 1° left”.

From Arad there are three roads (to Sibiu, Timișoara, Zerind), and none of them reaches the goal directly. Without a map the agent could only try roads at random. With a map, it can look ahead at future states and pick a sequence that ends in Bucharest. In general, an agent with several immediate options of unknown value can decide what to do by first examining future actions that eventually lead to states of known value.

  • The process of looking for a sequence of actions that reaches the goal is called search.
  • A search algorithm takes a problem as input and returns a solution in the form of an action sequence.
  • Once a solution is found, its actions are carried out. This is the execution phase.
The agent program and its assumptions

This simple design works only when the environment is:

  • fully observable (the agent knows its current state),
  • discrete (finitely many actions in each state),
  • known (it knows which state each action leads to),
  • and deterministic (each action has exactly one outcome).
Under these assumptions the solution is a fixed action sequence, and the agent can execute it “with its eyes closed”: control theorists call this an open-loop system, because percepts are ignored during execution.

AIMA Figure 3.1 : a simple problem-solving agent

function Simple-Problem-Solving-Agent(percept) returns an action persistent: seq, an action sequence, initially empty; state; goal; problem state ← Update-State(state, percept) if seq is empty then goal ← Formulate-Goal(state) problem ← Formulate-Problem(state, goal) seq ← Search(problem) if seq = failure then return a null action action ← First(seq);  seq ← Rest(seq) return action

How the agent program works

The key idea: the agent thinks once, then acts many times. On the first call it plans a whole route; on every later call it just hands out the next step of that plan, without thinking again.

An agent program is not called once to “solve the problem”. It is called repeatedly, once per time step. Each call receives the latest percept and must return exactly one action:

Read in that light, the pseudocode has four parts: a memory, a sensing step, a planning step that runs only sometimes, and an acting step that runs every time.

1. The agent’s memory

persistent: seq, an action sequence, initially empty; state; goal; problem

Persistent means these variables keep their values between calls, like static variables in C. Without this, the agent would forget its plan after every call and would have to search again each time.

  • seq is the plan still to be carried out. It starts empty, and an empty plan is what triggers planning.
  • state is the agent’s current belief about the world.
  • goal is what it is currently trying to achieve.
  • problem is the formal problem it built from that goal.

2. Sensing: update the state

state ← Update-State(state, percept)

The agent combines its previous belief with the new percept. In Romania, the percept “I am in Arad” becomes the state \(\textit{In}(\textit{Arad})\). This line runs on every call, but in this simple agent the updated state is only used when a new plan is made.

3. Planning: only when there is no plan left

if seq is empty then goal ← Formulate-Goal(state) problem ← Formulate-Problem(state, goal) seq ← Search(problem) if seq = failure then return a null action

This block runs only on the very first call, or after the previous plan has been used up. If seq still holds actions, the agent skips it entirely.

  • Formulate the goal. From its situation and performance measure the agent picks a concrete target. Holding a non-refundable ticket out of Bucharest, it adopts \(\textit{In}(\textit{Bucharest})\). This turns a vague performance measure into something search can aim at.
  • Formulate the problem. The agent builds the five components:
    • initial state \(\textit{In}(\textit{Arad})\)
    • actions such as \(\textit{Go}(\textit{Sibiu})\)
    • the transition model \(\textsf{RESULT}(s,a)\)
    • the goal test \(\textit{In}(\textit{Bucharest})\)
    • path cost as total road distance
    Choosing the level of detail (“drive to the next city”, not “turn the wheel 2°”) is where abstraction happens.
  • Search. Any search algorithm can be plugged in here: BFS, UCS, A*, and so on. It returns an action sequence that reaches the goal, for example \[[\,\textit{Go}(\textit{Sibiu}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Rimnicu Vilcea}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Pitesti}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Bucharest})\,]\] The agent doesn’t care which algorithm produced it. That separation is why every strategy in Part II fits into this one frame.
  • Handle failure. If no solution exists, the agent returns a null action (do nothing) rather than acting at random.

4. Acting: take the next step of the plan

action ← First(seq);  seq ← Rest(seq) return action

The agent removes the first action from the front of the plan, keeps the rest for later calls, and returns that single action. seq behaves like a queue consumed one item per call.

Tracing it over time

Callseq at the startWhat happensReturns
1emptyFormulate goal and problem; Search → [Sibiu, Rimnicu Vilcea, Pitesti, Bucharest]Go(Sibiu)
2[Rimnicu Vilcea, Pitesti, Bucharest]Skip planningGo(Rimnicu Vilcea)
3[Pitesti, Bucharest]Skip planningGo(Pitesti)
4[Bucharest]Skip planningGo(Bucharest)
5emptyPlan again from the new state…

Search runs once, on call 1. Calls 2 to 4 only execute the plan, so they are cheap.

Open loop: why the agent can ignore its percepts

On calls 2 to 4 the agent receives percepts and updates state, but never compares them with what it expected before acting. Control theorists call this an open-loop system. It is safe only under this chapter’s assumptions: the environment is fully observable, discrete, known and deterministic. Under those conditions the world unfolds exactly as planned, so checking is unnecessary.

Where it breaks

Suppose the road from Sibiu to Rimnicu Vilcea is closed. The agent still returns Go(Rimnicu Vilcea) on call 2, because nothing in this program notices that the plan has failed. The fix is a closed-loop agent that monitors its percepts during execution and replans when reality departs from the plan.

Common misconceptions

“It runs search on every call.” It doesn’t. Search runs only when seq is empty.

“state is updated, so the agent reacts to the world.” It is updated but not used while a plan is being executed. That is exactly what makes the agent open-loop.

“The problem is given to the agent.” The agent formulates it itself from state and goal. Formulation is part of the agent’s job, not an input.

“Search is a specific algorithm.” It is a placeholder for any search strategy.

The five components of a problem

A well-defined problem is specified by five components. For the Romania trip:

  1. Initial state — where the agent starts: \(\textit{In}(\textit{Arad})\).
  2. Actions — \(\textsf{ACTIONS}(s)\) returns the actions applicable in state \(s\). From \(\textit{In}(\textit{Arad})\): \(\{\textit{Go}(\textit{Sibiu}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Timisoara}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Zerind})\}\).
  3. Transition model — \(\textsf{RESULT}(s,a)\) returns the state reached by doing \(a\) in \(s\) (its successor): \[\textsf{RESULT}(\textit{In}(\textit{Arad}),\ \textit{Go}(\textit{Sibiu})) = \textit{In}(\textit{Sibiu})\] and likewise for Timișoara and Zerind.
  4. Goal test — decides whether a state is a goal: \(s = \textit{In}(\textit{Bucharest})\). The goal can also be given abstractly, e.g. “checkmate” in chess.
  5. Path cost — a function giving each path a numeric cost. Here it is the sum of the individual step costs \(c(s,a,s')\) along the path (road km). Step costs are assumed non-negative.
State space, Solutions, Abstraction

The initial state, actions and transition model together define the state space: the set of all states reachable from the initial state. It forms a directed graph (the Romania map is one, if each road is read as two directed edges). A path is a sequence of states connected by actions.

A solution is an action sequence from the initial state to a goal state; an optimal solution has the lowest path cost among all solutions.

Removing detail from a representation is abstraction. A good abstraction removes as much detail as possible while keeping the problem valid (every abstract solution can be expanded into a real one) and keeping its actions easy to carry out.

Example problems

The 8-puzzle

A 3×3 board with eight numbered tiles and one blank. A tile next to the blank can slide into it. The object is to reach a specified goal configuration, such as the one on the right. The standard formulation:

  • States: the location of each of the eight tiles and the blank in one of the nine squares.
  • Initial state: any state can be the initial state.
  • Actions: the simplest formulation treats them as movements of the blank: Left, Right, Up, Down. Fewer are available at an edge or corner.
  • Transition model: given a state and an action, returns the resulting state. Applying Left to the start state above swaps the 5 and the blank.
  • Goal test: checks whether the state matches the goal configuration.
  • Path cost: each step costs 1, so path cost = number of steps.

The 8-puzzle belongs to the family of sliding-block puzzles, which are NP-complete to solve optimally in general, so it is a standard test bed for search algorithms.

Why: read the tiles row by row, skipping the blank, and count the inversions, i.e. pairs of tiles that appear in the wrong order. A horizontal move does not change the reading order at all. A vertical move lifts one tile past exactly two others, which changes the inversion count by \(-2\), \(0\) or \(+2\). So the parity of the inversion count never changes.

The initial state 7 2 4 5 6 8 3 1 has 16 inversions (even), the goal 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 has 0 (even), and the twin 2 1 3 4 5 6 7 8 has 1 (odd). Every state lies in exactly one of two parity classes of equal size, which is why only \(9!/2\) states are reachable from any start.

Exercise: how many states does the 8-puzzle have?

Show the worked answer

Nine squares hold eight distinct tiles and a blank, so there are \(9! = 362{,}880\) arrangements in total.

But every move preserves a parity invariant: the state space splits into two disjoint halves, and no sequence of moves takes you from one half to the other. So from any start state exactly half the arrangements are reachable:

\[\frac{9!}{2} = 181{,}440 \text{ reachable states.}\]

For scale (AIMA §3.2): the 15-puzzle (4×4) has about \(1.3\times10^{12}\) reachable states, and the 24-puzzle (5×5) about \(10^{25}\).

Added · other standard problems

Vacuum world. Two squares, each dirty or clean, and the agent in one of them: \(2\times2^2 = 8\) states. Actions Left, Right, Suck; each step costs 1.

8-queens. Place 8 queens so none attacks another. An incremental formulation that adds queens to any empty square has \(64\cdot63\cdots57 \approx 1.8\times10^{14}\) sequences. Adding a queen only to the leftmost empty column, and only on a non-attacked square, cuts this to 2,057 states. The formulation matters enormously.

Real-world problems: route finding (navigation, airline travel planning), touring problems such as the travelling salesperson problem (TSP), VLSI layout, robot navigation, automatic assembly sequencing, and protein design.

Searching for solutions: tree search and graph search

A solution is an action sequence, so search algorithms consider the possible sequences starting from the initial state. They form a search tree: the root is the initial state, branches are actions, and nodes are states.

Expanding a node means applying every legal action to its state, generating a child node for each. The set of all leaf nodes available for expansion at any moment is the frontier (also called the open list). Search algorithms differ only in which frontier node they expand next: this choice is the search strategy.

AIMA Figure 3.7 - Tree search

Which leaf is “chosen” decides the algorithm.:

Why tree search can loop

  • Tree search does not remember which states it has already visited, so it can generate the same state many times through redundant paths.
  • A loopy path such as Arad → Sibiu → Arad is a special case. Loops make the tree infinite even though the Romania map has only 20 states.
  • The fix: keep track of visited states. That remembered set is the explored set (also called the closed list).
How bad redundant paths get

On a rectangular grid, each state has 4 successors, so a search tree of depth \(d\) has \(4^d\) leaves. Yet only about \(2d^2\) distinct states lie within \(d\) steps. For \(d = 20\) that is roughly a trillion nodes covering only about 800 states. Remembering visited states turns an exponential search into a polynomial one here.

Infrastructure for search algorithms

Each node \(n\) of the search tree is a data structure with four components:

  • n.STATE: the state in the state space that the node corresponds to;
  • n.PARENT: the node in the search tree that generated this node;
  • n.ACTION: the action applied to the parent to generate this node;
  • n.PATH-COST: the cost, written \(g(n)\), of the path from the initial state to the node, following parent pointers.

Child-node creation from a parent node

Measuring problem-solving performance

  • Completeness: is the algorithm guaranteed to find a solution when there is one?
  • Optimality: does the strategy find the optimal solution (lowest path cost among all solutions)?
  • Time complexity: how long does it take to find a solution? Measured as the number of nodes generated.
  • Space complexity: how much memory is needed to perform the search? Measured as the maximum number of nodes stored.

Because state spaces in AI are often implicit and possibly infinite, complexity is expressed with three quantities:

  • \(b\): the branching factor, the maximum number of successors of any node;
  • \(d\): the depth of the shallowest goal node (the number of steps along the path from the root);
  • \(m\): the maximum length of any path in the state space (can be \(\infty\)).
Part II · Lecture 2

Uninformed search strategies

Uninformed (blind) search

  • Has no additional information about states beyond what the problem definition gives.
  • Can only generate successors and distinguish a goal state from a non-goal state.
  • Strategies that know whether one non-goal state is “more promising” than another are called informed or heuristic search strategies (the next chapter: greedy best-first, A*).

All the strategies below are distinguished only by the order in which nodes are expanded.

1. Breadth-first search (BFS)

The root is expanded first, then all of its successors, then their successors, and so on. All nodes at depth \(k\) are expanded before any node at depth \(k+1\). BFS is graph search with a FIFO queue as the frontier.

AIMA Figure 3.11 Peter Norvig

BFS(G, s) CLRS

The two versions line up through CLRS’s vertex colours:

  • White = undiscovered (in neither the frontier nor the explored set);
  • Gray = frontier (in the queue);
  • Black = explored (in the explored set).

Norvig’s test “child not in explored or frontier” is exactly CLRS’s test “v.color == WHITE”. CLRS has no goal test because it computes shortest-path distances to every vertex.

Why BFS finds the shallowest goal

Time complexity

In the worst case the goal is the last node generated at depth \(d\). The total number of nodes generated is a geometric progression:

\[ N_{\text{BFS}} = 1 + b + b^2 + \cdots + b^d = \frac{b^{d+1}-1}{b-1} \;\approx\; \frac{b^{d+1}}{b} = b^d \quad(\text{using } b-1\approx b) \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; O(b^d). \]

Space is also \(O(b^d)\): every generated node stays in memory, \(O(b^{d-1})\) in the explored set and \(O(b^d)\) on the frontier. Memory, not time, is the real problem with BFS.

Complete if \(b\) is finite. *Optimal only if path cost is a non-decreasing function of depth, e.g. when all step costs are equal. On Romania, BFS returns Arad → Sibiu → Fagaras → Bucharest (3 steps, 450 km), not the cheapest route (418 km).

2. Uniform-cost search (UCS)

Instead of the shallowest node, UCS expands the node \(n\) with the lowest path cost \(g(n)\). The frontier is a priority queue ordered by \(g\).

AIMA Figure 3.14 Peter Norvig

Two differences from BFS, both highlighted:

  1. The goal test runs when a node is selected for expansion, not when it is generated. The first generated goal may lie on a sub-optimal path.
  2. If a cheaper path to a state already on the frontier is found, the frontier node is replaced. The frontier must therefore support fast membership tests: a priority queue combined with a hash table.

Relation to Dijkstra’s algorithm CLRS

UCS vs. Dijkstra

They follow the same idea: repeatedly settle the vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relax its edges. The differences are practical. Dijkstra puts every vertex in the queue at the start and runs until all shortest paths from \(s\) are known. UCS adds states lazily as they are generated (the graph may be implicit or infinite), and it stops as soon as a goal is popped. UCS’s “replace that frontier node with a cheaper child” plays the role of RELAX plus DECREASE-KEY.

Complexity in terms of \(C^*\) and \(\epsilon\)

  • \(C^*\) is the cost of the optimal solution.
  • UCS works on a weighted graph and is guided by path cost, not depth, so its time and space cannot be expressed in terms of \(d\) or \(m\) alone. We use \(C^*\) as the measure instead.
  • Assume every step costs at least some positive constant \(\epsilon > 0\).
  • Then the optimal path has at most \(k\) steps, where \(k\cdot\epsilon = C^*\):
\[ k\cdot\epsilon = C^* \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{C^*}{\epsilon} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{Time} = \text{Space} = O\!\left(b^{\,1+\lfloor C^*/\epsilon\rfloor}\right) \]

So \(C^*/\epsilon\) plays the role that \(d\) played in BFS. The extra \(+1\) appears because UCS tests the goal only on expansion, so it generates (and must store) one more layer of nodes beyond the goal’s cost level. When all step costs are equal, \(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\epsilon\rfloor}\) is just \(b^{d+1}\). UCS can be much worse than BFS: it may explore large trees of cheap, useless steps before trying a path with one expensive but useful step.

CompleteYes*
OptimalYes
Time\(O(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\epsilon\rfloor})\)
Space\(O(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\epsilon\rfloor})\)

*Complete if \(b\) is finite and every step cost is \(\geq \epsilon > 0\). Optimal in general: whenever UCS selects a node for expansion, the optimal path to it has been found.

3. Depth-first search (DFS)

DFS always expands the deepest node on the frontier. It is graph or tree search with a LIFO queue (stack): the most recently generated node is chosen first. When it reaches a node with no successors, it “backs up” to the next deepest node that still has unexplored successors. (Often implemented recursively.)

DFS(G) CLRS

Why DFS is not optimal

Completeness. It depends on the version.

  • Graph-search DFS is complete in finite state spaces: it eventually expands every node.
  • Tree-search DFS is not complete even then: on Romania it can loop Arad → Sibiu → Arad forever. (Checking new states against the current path fixes loops but not redundant paths.)
  • In infinite state spaces both versions fail if an infinite non-goal path is encountered.

Time is \(O(b^m)\), possibly much larger than the state space, and terrible if \(m \gg d\).

Space is where DFS shines. Tree-search DFS needs to store only one root-to-leaf path plus the unexpanded siblings of each node on it: \(O(bm)\). With \(d = 16\) and the Fig. 3.13 assumptions that is 156 KB instead of 10 EB.

Tree search DFS

4. Depth-limited search (DLS)

DFS fails in infinite state spaces. DLS fixes this by giving DFS a predetermined depth limit \(\ell\): nodes at depth \(\ell\) are treated as if they have no successors.

AIMA Figure 3.17 — recursive depth-limited tree search

Cutoff vs. failure, and choosing ℓ

DLS can end two ways. failure means there is no solution at all; cutoff means there is no solution within the depth limit. Iterative deepening depends on this distinction.

DLS is incomplete if \(\ell < d\) (the shallowest goal is beyond the limit) and non-optimal if \(\ell > d\). Domain knowledge can set \(\ell\): Romania has 20 cities, so any solution has length at most 19. Better still, any city can reach any other in at most 9 steps. This number, the diameter of the state space, gives a tighter limit \(\ell = 9\).

DFS is the special case \(\ell = \infty\).

CompleteNo*
OptimalNo
Time\(O(b^\ell)\)
Space\(O(b\ell)\)

*Complete if \(\ell \geq d\).

5. Iterative deepening depth-first search (IDS)

Run DLS with limit 0, then 1, then 2, … until a goal is found. It combines the benefits of both:

BFS
DFS
Time \(O(b^d)\)
Time \(O(b^m)\)
Space \(O(b^d)\)
Space \(O(bm)\)

IDS takes the boxed winner from each column: BFS’s time, and DFS-like linear space (\(O(bd)\), since it never goes deeper than \(d\)).

AIMA Figure 3.18

It terminates when a solution is found, or when DLS returns failure, meaning no solution exists.

Is repeating the shallow levels wasteful?

Nodes at depth \(k\) are generated once in each iteration with limit \(\geq k\). With a goal at depth \(d\), the bottom level is generated once, the next one up twice, and so on. The root’s children are generated \(d\) times (the root itself is never “generated”):

\[ X = d\,b + (d-1)\,b^2 + (d-2)\,b^3 + \cdots + 1\cdot b^d = \sum_{k=1}^{d}(d-k+1)\,b^k . \]

Time complexity, derived

Use the shift-and-subtract trick for arithmetico-geometric series. Multiply by \(b\):

\[ \begin{aligned} X &= d\,b + (d-1)\,b^2 + (d-2)\,b^3 + \cdots + 2\,b^{d-1} + b^d &&(1)\\ bX &= \phantom{d\,b + {}} d\,b^2 + (d-1)\,b^3 + \cdots + 3\,b^{d-1} + 2\,b^d + b^{d+1} &&(2) \end{aligned} \]

Subtract (1) from (2). Matching powers of \(b\) differ by exactly 1 in their coefficients:

\[ (b-1)X = -d\,b + \underbrace{\left(b^2 + b^3 + \cdots + b^{d+1}\right)}_{\text{G.P.}} = -d\,b + \frac{b^{d+2}-b^2}{b-1} \] \[ \boxed{\,X = \frac{b^{d+2}-b^2}{(b-1)^2} - \frac{d\,b}{b-1}\,} \;\approx\; b^d\left(\frac{b}{b-1}\right)^{2} \;=\; O(b^d) \]

Check with \(b=2, d=2\): direct count \(2\cdot2 + 1\cdot4 = 8\); formula \(\frac{16-4}{1} - \frac{4}{1} = 8\). ✓

Numerically, for \(b = 10, d = 5\):

\[ N(\text{IDS}) = 50 + 400 + 3{,}000 + 20{,}000 + 100{,}000 = 123{,}450 \qquad N(\text{BFS}) = 10 + 100 + 1{,}000 + 10{,}000 + 100{,}000 = 111{,}110 \]

Only about 11% overhead. Most of the nodes are at the bottom level, so repeating the upper levels barely matters. In general the overhead ratio tends to \(b/(b-1)\).

Rule of thumb

Iterative deepening is the preferred uninformed method when the search space is large and the depth of the solution is unknown.

CompleteYes*
OptimalYes†
Time\(O(b^d)\)
Space\(O(bd)\)

*Complete if \(b\) is finite. †Optimal if all step costs are identical (same condition as BFS).

6. Bidirectional search

Run two simultaneous searches, one forward from the initial state and one backward from the goal, and stop when the two frontiers meet. The motivation is that \(b^{d/2} + b^{d/2}\) is much less than \(b^d\). For \(b=10, d=6\): BFS generates about a million nodes, bidirectional BFS about 2,220.

The goal test is replaced by a check for whether the two frontiers intersect; if they do, a solution has been found. With a hash table, that check takes constant time per node.

Requirements and caveats
  • Predecessors must be computable. Searching backward needs the predecessors of a state. Easy when actions are reversible (Romania roads); hard otherwise.
  • The goal must be explicit. With one or a few explicit goal states (Bucharest), backward search is easy. A goal described abstractly, such as “no queen attacks another” in 8-queens, gives no state to start from.
  • The first meeting is not always the shortest path. Even with BFS in both directions, an extra check is needed to make sure no shortcut exists across the gap.
  • Memory. At least one frontier must be kept in memory for the intersection check, which is the main weakness of the \(O(b^{d/2})\) space.
CompleteYes*
OptimalYes†
Time\(O(b^{d/2})\)
Space\(O(b^{d/2})\)

*If \(b\) is finite and both directions use BFS. †If step costs are identical and both directions use BFS.

Choosing between the algorithms

Large search spaces with a wide branching factor but a bounded depth

TSP is the classic example. With 50 cities, every complete tour is a leaf at depth 50, but the number of orderings is enormous: \(50!\) sequences, or \((n-1)!/2 = 49!/2\) distinct tours once you fix the starting city and ignore direction. (The branching factor is large near the root and shrinks by one at each level.)

  • In such cases DF-BB (depth-first branch-and-bound) works very well. DFS has modest space requirements, and the bounding step prunes many branches.
  • Iterative deepening looks attractive for its space, but in TSP all solutions lie at the leaves (depth \(n\)). IDS would re-search every shallower level before reaching the only level that matters, so DF-BB beats IDS here.
What depth-first branch-and-bound is

DF-BB runs DFS but remembers the cost \(U\) of the best complete solution found so far (initially \(U = \infty\)). Whenever a partial path’s cost \(g(n)\) (or a lower bound on its completion, \(g(n)+h(n)\)) is already \(\geq U\), that whole subtree is pruned, because it cannot beat the incumbent. Each new better solution lowers \(U\) and makes pruning more aggressive. It keeps DFS’s \(O(bm)\) memory and, if run to completion, returns an optimal solution.

Large depth with a modest branching factor

  • Goal nodes may lie close to the root while the space itself is very deep (or infinite). DFS may wander down a deep branch for a long time (or forever) before reaching the goal; BFS, which finds the shallowest goal, may do better.
  • If memory is the constraint, IDS gives the same shallowest-goal guarantee in linear space.
Quick decision guide
SituationGood choice
Unit step costs, small \(d\), plenty of memoryBFS
Varying step costs, need the cheapest pathUCS
Large space, solution depth unknown, little memoryIDS
Known bound on solution depthDLS with \(\ell\) = diameter
All solutions at a fixed depth, optimisation (TSP)DF-BB
Single explicit goal, reversible actionsBidirectional BFS
